lessons.title: Linguistic diversity and dialects
lessons.anelcac: Notions of linguistic diversity, dialects, names of languages, geographical classification
objectives: Becoming aware of the linguistic diversity of Cameroon (about 280 languages according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas)
Distinguish language, dialect and variant according to academic definitions
Naming Èwòndó and locating it in the geographical classification of the languages of Cameroon
Adopt an attitude of respect towards all languages

teacher.intro: Lesson: Linguistic diversity and dialects. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Display the map of the Linguistic Mini-Atlas of Cameroon. Ask students which languages are spoken in their family.
**Exploration:** Have students read the definitions in the Mini-Atlas (language, dialect, patois, national language). Locate Èwòndó in its linguistic region.
**Conceptualisation:** Explain the language / dialect distinction with examples: the Bulu, Ewondo, Eton and Mangisa dialects all belong to the Beti-Fang language (Mini-Atlas).
**Application:** Complete a table: name of the language, family, main region, ISO code.
**Assessment:** Each student gives an oral presentation of Èwòndó, indicating family and region.
teacher.freedom: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.
teacher.tips: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.

student.intro: Cameroon is one of the richest nations in the world in languages — the linguistic Mini-Atlas lists about 280! In this lesson, you discover the place of Èwòndó in this great family.
activities: Look at the Mini-Atlas map and find the area where Èwòndó is mainly spoken.
Copy and complete: Èwòndó belongs to the ___ family. It is mostly spoken in the ___ region.
According to the Mini-Atlas, how many living languages are there in the Èwòndó region? Note down this number.
Survey: ask an adult the name of the language in which they were raised and where it is spoken.
Memorise: **dialect** = an intelligible variant of the same language; **national language** = language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State (ACA LAN).
student.memo: Cameroon has about **280 languages** according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas. Èwòndó belongs to a Cameroonian language family and has its own dialectal variants. According to the ACA LAN, a national language is the language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State.

lessons.title: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas
lessons.anelcac: Classification of the languages of Cameroon: linguistic areas, families, ALCAM atlas
objectives: Name the main linguistic areas of Cameroon
Read and interpret an extract from a linguistic atlas (ALCAM / Mini-Atlas)
Classify Èwòndó according to its typological criteria
Producing a short text presenting Èwòndó

teacher.intro: Lesson: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Go back over the definitions. How many language families do students remember?
**Presentation:** The 8 world language families according to Ethnologue (Niger-Kordofanian, Nilo-Saharan, Afro-Asiatic…). Place Cameroonian languages within this whole.
**Explanation:** Show how to find Èwòndó in the ALCAM: ISO code, family, location.
**Guided practice:** In pairs, students find 3 languages neighbouring Èwòndó and note their ISO codes.
**Production:** 5-line paragraph presenting Èwòndó (family, region, speakers, distinctive feature).
teacher.freedom: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.
teacher.tips: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.

student.intro: A linguistic atlas is a specialised map. The ALCAM (Atlas of the Languages of Cameroon) and the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas let you locate Èwòndó precisely.
activities: On the Mini-Atlas map, locate Èwòndó and note its administrative region.
List 3 languages whose area is adjacent to that of Èwòndó.
Classify these 4 languages in a table: Language | Family | Main region.
Write an introductory paragraph about Èwòndó with at least 5 pieces of information taken from the atlas.
Memorise: **ISO 639** = international language codes; **ALCAM** = Atlas des Langues du Cameroun.
student.memo: The **ALCAM** and the **LACAGEO Mini-Atlas** list and locate all the national languages of Cameroon. Cameroon has 8 main language families. Èwòndó appears there with its family and its location. Knowing how to read a linguistic atlas is reading the history of peoples.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Vowels of Èwòndó
lessons.anelcac: AGLC vowels — simple, specific, complex
objectives: Identify the simple vowels of the phonological system of Èwòndó
Recognising specific vowels absent from French
Pronouncing vowels correctly in the context of a word
Transcribing words containing vowels according to AGLC

teacher.intro: Lesson: Èwòndó vowels. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write known words in Èwòndó on the board and ask which sounds students hear.
**Presentation:** Introduce the AGLC. Write the simple vowels of Èwòndó on the board, articulating them clearly.
**Explanation:** Vowels specific to Èwòndó that are absent from French (nasal, particular openness…). Listening and repetition exercises.
**Application:** List of 10 words — students underline the vowels and indicate: simple or specific.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 simple words — students transcribe them with the correct vowels.
teacher.freedom: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.
teacher.tips: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.

student.intro: Every language has its own sounds. In Èwòndó, some vowels do not exist in French. This lesson teaches you to hear, pronounce and write them.
activities: Listen to the recordings of the Èwòndó vocabulary and identify the vowels you hear.
Classify the vowels: **Shared with French** | **Specific to Èwòndó**.
Transcribe the 5 dictated words, taking care to note each vowel correctly.
Find 3 words in Èwòndó for each specific vowel and write them down.
Memorise: **AGLC** = Alphabet Général des Langues Camerounaises, the official reference.
student.memo: The vowel system of **Èwòndó** includes simple vowels and specific vowels (e.g. nasalised vowels). They are written using the **AGLC**. Mastery of vowels is the basis of reading and writing in Èwòndó.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Èwòndó consonants and written production
lessons.anelcac: Consonants — simple, specific, complex; written production of vowels and consonants
objectives: Identify the consonant system of Èwòndó
Recognising specific consonants absent from French
Articulate consonants correctly in context
Writing words with vowels and consonants correctly notated

teacher.intro: Lesson: Èwòndó consonants and written production. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the vowels. What is a consonant?
**Presentation:** Table of Èwòndó consonants according to the AGLC. Stress the specific consonants (labio-velars, prenasalised, implosives…).
**Explanation:** Articulating difficult consonants: in isolation → syllable → word.
**Application:** Minimal pairs: listening to words that differ only by one consonant.
**Production:** 5 simple sentences in Èwòndó with careful consonant transcription.
teacher.freedom: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.
teacher.tips: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.

student.intro: After the vowels, here are the consonants of Èwòndó! Some are unique — you will only hear them in Èwòndó and in a few neighbouring African languages.
activities: Listen to the minimal pairs and tick the word you hear (e.g. bìlí / pìlí).
Transcribe 5 dictated words, paying attention to the specific consonants.
Find in the vocabulary all the words containing a prenasalised consonant. How many do you find?
Compose 3 simple sentences in Èwòndó, each with at least one specific consonant.
Memorise: **minimal pair** = two words identical except for one phoneme.
student.memo: The consonant system of **Èwòndó** includes consonants shared with French and specific consonants (implosives, prenasalised, labio-velars…). Writing them according to the **AGLC** is essential for reading and writing.

lessons.title: Definition and functions of tones
lessons.anelcac: Tones — definition, function, presentation; simple tones (high, low, mid)
objectives: Define tone as a distinctive feature of tone languages
Distinguish lexical tone from grammatical tone
Identify the simple tones of Èwòndó
Transcribing words with their tones according to AGLC

teacher.intro: Lesson: Definition and function of tones. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Say two Èwòndó words that are written the same but have different tones and different meanings.
**Presentation:** Define tone. Present the simple tones of Èwòndó and their AGLC diacritics.
**Explanation:** Simple tones: high (´), low (`), mid (¯). Have students repeat each tone.
**Application:** Match recorded words with their tone notation.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 words — students note the tones.
teacher.freedom: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.
teacher.tips: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.

student.intro: Èwòndó is a tonal language: the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of the word! You will learn to hear and write down these tones.
activities: Listen to the pairs of words. For each pair, are the tones the same or different?
Transcribe 5 words with their tones using the AGLC diacritics (´ ` ¯).
Find 2 words in the vocabulary that differ only in tone. What does each one mean?
Sing the tones of a 3-syllable word as High-Low-High, then Low-High-Low. What difference do you hear?
Memorise: high tone = ´ ; low tone = ` ; mid tone = ¯.
student.memo: In **Èwòndó**, tone is phonological: it distinguishes words with different meanings. The **simple tones** are high (´), low (`), and sometimes mid (¯). They are written using the **AGLC** diacritics.

lessons.title: Complex tones and tone-marked written production
lessons.anelcac: Complex tones (rising, falling); finding the tone of a word; tonal written production
objectives: Identify the complex tones of Èwòndó (rising, falling)
Finding the tone of a word by the isolation method
Transcribing sentences with full tone marking
Producing a short text in Èwòndó with correct tones

teacher.intro: Lesson: Complex tones and tonal written production. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the simple tones. Announce that some syllables carry two tones in succession.
**Presentation:** Complex tones: falling (̂), rising (̌). Let students hear them and reproduce them.
**Explanation:** Isolation method: say the word with an artificial high tone, then a low one, and listen to which sounds natural.
**Application:** Students find the tone of 10 words in Èwòndó using the isolation method.
**Production:** Dialogue of 6 lines in Èwòndó with complete tone notation.
teacher.freedom: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.
teacher.tips: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.

student.intro: You know the simple tones. Now for the complex tones of Èwòndó — syllables that rise and fall at the same time!
activities: Listen to the recorded words and sort them: Simple tone | Complex tone.
Apply the isolation method to 5 words: say them high, then low, and note the tone you perceive.
Transcribe a dialogue of 4 lines in Èwòndó with all the tones marked.
Write a 3-sentence text in Èwòndó about an action from your daily life, with tone marking.
Memorise: falling tone = ̂ ; rising tone = ̌.
student.memo: The **complex tones** of **Èwòndó** (falling ̂, rising ̌) are melodic movements on a single syllable. The **isolation method** makes it possible to find the tone of an unknown word. A transcription in Èwòndó without tones is incomplete.

lessons.title: The noun base and noun classes
lessons.anelcac: NP: constituents, base noun + affixes, noun classes, personal pronouns
objectives: Identify the structure of the noun in Èwòndó (base + affixes)
Recognising the noun classes of Èwòndó
Form the singular and plural of nouns
Use the personal pronouns corresponding to noun classes

teacher.intro: Lesson: The noun base and noun classes. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a noun in Èwòndó in the singular and plural. What changes?
**Presentation:** Noun class: in Bantu and Bantoid languages, nouns are grouped into classes marked by prefixes.
**Explanation:** Main noun classes of Èwòndó with singular and plural prefixes.
**Application:** Table: singular → plural for 10 nouns.
**Assessment:** Identify the noun class of 5 nouns.
teacher.freedom: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).
teacher.tips: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).

student.intro: In Èwòndó, nouns are organised into **classes**. Each class has its own prefixes for the singular and plural — a much richer system than gender in French!
activities: Using the Èwòndó vocabulary, make a table: Singular | Plural | Noun class.
Identify the class prefix in each noun. Highlight it.
Put the following 5 nouns into the plural by changing the prefix according to the class.
Match each noun with its corresponding class pronoun.
Memorise: **noun class** = grammatical category of nouns, marked by prefixes.
student.memo: In **Èwòndó**, nouns are organised into **noun classes** marked by prefixes. A change of prefix indicates number. Pronouns, adjectives and verbs agree with the class of the noun.

lessons.title: Noun determiners
lessons.anelcac: Determiners: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives; noun class agreement
objectives: Identify the different types of determiners in Èwòndó
Make determiners agree with the noun according to the noun class
Build complex noun phrases
Producing sentences with complete NPs

vocabulary.langText: à ngá   bə́   bə̀↓lə́ ɛ̀ngə̀g ńló  àì    àyǎp kíŋ.
vocabulary.frenchText: he had a big head and a long neck.

vocabulary.langText: à ngá   bə́   bə̀↓lə́ ɛ̀ngə̀g ǹnló  àì    àyǎp kíŋ.
vocabulary.frenchText: he had a big head and a long neck.

vocabulary.langText: mìmvɔ̀ á də́ mié  mí nə̀ víndì

teacher.intro: Lesson: Noun determiners. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a simple noun phrase. How can it be enriched?
**Presentation:** Determiners in Èwòndó: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives.
**Explanation:** Each determiner agrees with the class of the noun (same class prefix or suffix).
**Application:** Complete noun phrases with the correct determiner according to the class.
**Production:** 5 complex noun phrases (noun + 2 determiners) used in sentences.
teacher.freedom: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Èwòndó compared with French.
teacher.tips: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Èwòndó compared with French.

student.intro: A noun with its determiners becomes much more precise! In Èwòndó, determiners agree with the **noun class**.
activities: Complete the NPs with the correct possessive determiner according to the noun class.
Underline the determiners in 5 sentences in Èwòndó and identify their type.
Turn each simple noun phrase into a complex noun phrase by adding a demonstrative and a numeral.
Write 5 sentences in Èwòndó with at least two determiners per noun phrase.
Memorise: **class agreement** = the determiner changes form according to the noun class.
student.memo: In **Èwòndó**, all determiners (possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives) agree with the **noun class** of the noun. A **complex NP** = noun + nominal base + agreeing determiners.

lessons.title: The verb stem and conjugation
lessons.anelcac: VP: constituents, stem, affixes, conjugation, verb tenses
objectives: Identify the verb stem and the conjugation affixes in Èwòndó
Conjugate a verb in the main tenses
Analyse the morphological structure of a verb form
Use verb forms correctly in sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The verb stem and conjugation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a verb form in Èwòndó and ask students to identify the stem.
**Presentation:** Break down a verb form: subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes.
**Explanation:** Conjugation paradigm of a common verb in Èwòndó in several tenses.
**Application:** Conjugation table: 3 common verbs.
**Assessment:** Translate 5 sentences from French into Èwòndó.
teacher.freedom: The TAM system of Èwòndó is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.
teacher.tips: The TAM system of Èwòndó is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.

student.intro: The verb is the heart of the sentence in Èwòndó. It alone carries tense, aspect, mood and subject! In this lesson, you take apart the verbal mechanics.
activities: Break down 5 verb forms in Èwòndó: subject prefix | TAM marker | stem | suffix.
Conjugate the verb 'to eat' in Èwòndó in 3 different tenses for all persons.
Identify the tense of 5 sentences in Èwòndó and justify your answer.
Translate 3 sentences from French into Èwòndó, taking care with the conjugation.
Memorise: **TAM** = Tense-Aspect-Mood; this is what verbal affixes express in Èwòndó.
student.memo: In **Èwòndó**, a verb form = subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes. The **TAM** (Tense-Aspect-Mood) system expresses more precise temporal and aspectual nuances than in French.

lessons.title: Verbal moods and negation
lessons.anelcac: Moods: indicative, imperative; negation; written production of simple/complex VP
objectives: Identify and use the main verbal moods of Èwòndó
Form the verbal negation
Build simple and complex verb phrases
Producing a text with a variety of moods and aspects

teacher.intro: Lesson: Verbal moods and negation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Give an order in Èwòndó. Which mood is used?
**Presentation:** Moods in Èwòndó: indicative, imperative, and other aspectual moods.
**Explanation:** Formation of the negative in Èwòndó: prefix, negative suffix, or particle.
**Application:** Turn 5 affirmative sentences into negative ones and vice versa.
**Production:** 8-sentence text alternating affirmation, negation and imperative.
teacher.freedom: Negation in Èwòndó can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.
teacher.tips: Negation in Èwòndó can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.

student.intro: Giving an order, expressing doubt, denying an action — each nuance has its own form in Èwòndó!
activities: Put the 5 given sentences into the negative form.
Turn these 5 statements into imperatives addressed to a friend.
Identify the mood and polarity (affirmative/negative) of each sentence in the text provided.
Write a dialogue of 6 lines including at least 2 imperatives and 2 negations.
Memorise: **mood** = the way of viewing the action; **negation** = grammatical marker denying the action.
student.memo: In **Èwòndó**, the main moods are the **indicative** and the **imperative**. **Negation** is marked by a particle or a specific affix. The diversity of moods is an expressive richness of Èwòndó.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Èwòndó
lessons.title: The simple sentence and its types
lessons.anelcac: Simple, interrogative, negative and imperative sentence; word order
objectives: Analyse the structure of the simple sentence in Èwòndó
Distinguish the 4 types of sentences
Mastering the order of constituents
Producing varied simple sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The simple sentence and its types. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Èwòndó.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a sentence in Èwòndó. Who does what?
**Presentation:** Basic constituent order in Èwòndó. Compare with French.
**Explanation:** The 4 sentence types from the same basic sentence.
**Application:** Turn declarative sentences into interrogative ones, then into negative ones.
**Production:** 8 varied sentences (2 per type) about school life.
teacher.freedom: Word order in Èwòndó may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.
teacher.tips: Word order in Èwòndó may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.

student.intro: A well-constructed sentence in Èwòndó follows precise rules. You learn the types of sentences and word order.
activities: Identify the order of constituents in 5 sentences in Èwòndó.
Turn 4 declarative sentences into yes/no questions.
Turn these 4 sentences into negatives.
Write 2 sentences of each type (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative).
Memorise: the basic order in **Èwòndó** is typologically stable.
student.memo: The **simple sentence** in **Èwòndó** has a characteristic order of constituents. The 4 types (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative) are formed with specific grammatical markers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Èwòndó
lessons.title: Logical connectors and the complex sentence
lessons.anelcac: Logical connectors, complex sentence, coordination, subordination; written production
objectives: Identify the logical connectors of Èwòndó
Distinguish coordination from subordination
Build complex sentences
Producing a coherent text with syntactic variety

teacher.intro: Lesson: Logical connectors and the complex sentence. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Èwòndó.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a short story in Èwòndó. Which words link the sentences?
**Presentation:** Connectors in Èwòndó: coordinating and subordinating conjunctions.
**Explanation:** Complex sentence by coordination / by subordination. Examples in Èwòndó.
**Application:** Link 5 pairs of simple sentences with the appropriate connector.
**Production:** 10-sentence text on 'A day in my village' with 5 different connectors.
teacher.freedom: The connectors of Èwòndó often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.
teacher.tips: The connectors of Èwòndó often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.

student.intro: To tell stories and argue, you need to link your sentences. The **logical connectors** of Èwòndó are your tools!
activities: Underline all the connectors in the text provided.
Classify them: Addition | Cause | Consequence | Opposition | Time.
Link 5 pairs of sentences with the most appropriate connector.
Write a text of 8 sentences with at least 4 different connectors.
Memorise: coordination = same level; subordination = one sentence inside another.
student.memo: In **Èwòndó**, **logical connectors** make it possible to build coherent **complex sentences**. Varying syntactic structures improves the quality of written and spoken expression.

lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Èwòndó
lessons.anelcac: Everyday communication situations: greetings, introductions, polite expressions
objectives: Mastering greeting formulas according to context
Introducing yourself and someone else in Èwòndó
Use polite and respectful expressions
Holding a short everyday conversation

teacher.intro: Lesson: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Èwòndó. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Two students meet at the market. Act out the scene in French, then ask how to say it in Èwòndó.
**Presentation:** Greetings in Èwòndó according to the time of day, age and context.
**Explanation:** Formulas of respect towards elders, specific to Èwòndó culture.
**Role play:** In groups of 2, simulate encounters in various contexts (market, school, ceremony).
**Production:** Dialogue of 10 lines between two people of different generations.
teacher.freedom: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.
teacher.tips: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.

student.intro: Knowing how to greet in Èwòndó means respecting the culture! The greetings change depending on whom you greet and at what time.
activities: Complete the table of Èwòndó greetings: Time | Formula | Expected response.
Play role A: greeting an elder at the morning market.
Make up a dialogue of 8 lines between a child and their grandfather.
Note down 3 Èwòndó politeness formulas with no direct equivalent in French.
Memorise the morning and evening greeting formulas, and those for elders, in Èwòndó.
student.memo: **Greetings** in **Èwòndó** vary according to the time of day, status and social context. They reflect the community's values of respect and solidarity.

lessons.title: Express everyday needs and actions
lessons.anelcac: Real-life situations: shopping, requests for help, travelling, daily activities
objectives: Express everyday needs in Èwòndó
Describe daily activities
Use vocabulary for places and actions of everyday life
Producing a descriptive text on a typical day

teacher.intro: Lesson: Expressing everyday needs and actions. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Images of scenes from daily life — market, field, school, home. How can they be described in Èwòndó?
**Presentation:** Thematic vocabulary: food, travel, household activities.
**Simulation:** Market scene: buyer and seller in Èwòndó.
**Application:** Describe your day in Èwòndó (from waking up to going to bed).
**Production:** 10-sentence text: 'My day in Èwòndó'.
teacher.freedom: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.
teacher.tips: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.

student.intro: You know how to greet people. Now you are going to manage in everyday situations in Èwòndó: at the market, on the road, at home.
activities: Match each picture of a scene from daily life with the corresponding word or sentence in Èwòndó.
Play the role of the seller at the market: answer the requests in Èwòndó.
Write 5 sentences describing your morning activities from the time you wake up.
Translate these 5 sentences about daily journeys into Èwòndó.
Memorise 10 everyday words in Èwòndó with their French translation.
student.memo: The **everyday** vocabulary in **Èwòndó** covers food, getting around and household activities. Mastering it allows functional communication in all contexts.

lessons.title: Argue and persuade in Èwòndó
lessons.anelcac: Elaborate communication: argumentation, narration, formal speech
objectives: Build a simple argument in Èwòndó
Use the expressions of formal speech
Narrating a past event coherently
Delivering a 2-minute oral speech in Èwòndó

teacher.intro: Lesson: Arguing and persuading in Èwòndó. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a proverb in Èwòndó. Ask students to explain it and defend it.
**Presentation:** Formulas of formal oral speech in Èwòndó: forms of address, opening, closing.
**Explanation:** Structure of an argument: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion.
**Practice:** Debate: for or against the use of Èwòndó at school? Each group defends its position.
**Production:** 2-minute speech on a given theme.
teacher.freedom: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.
teacher.tips: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.

student.intro: In Èwòndó cultures, well-spoken words are a force. You learn to argue and persuade with eloquence.
activities: Identify in the text: thesis, arguments, examples.
Prepare 3 arguments to defend the teaching of Èwòndó in primary school.
Give an opening speech for a ceremony in Èwòndó.
Narration: tell in Èwòndó about a memorable event from your school life.
Memorise the opening and closing formulas of a formal speech in Èwòndó.
student.memo: **Argumentation** in **Èwòndó** follows this pattern: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion. **Formal speech** follows precise cultural conventions. Mastery of elaborate oral expression is a high-level skill.

lessons.title: Oral literature and advanced written production
lessons.anelcac: Oral literature: proverbs, tales, riddles; long written production
objectives: Analyse the structure of a tale or a riddle in Èwòndó
Identify the themes and values conveyed
Writing a short tale following the conventions of the genre
Using oral literature as a teaching resource

teacher.intro: Lesson: Oral literature and advanced written production. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Tell or play a short tale in Èwòndó.
**Presentation:** Genres of oral literature: tales, proverbs, riddles, epics.
**Analysis:** Structure of the tale: initial situation → disruption → events → resolution → moral.
**Application:** Analyse a tale provided, following this structure.
**Production:** Tale of at least 15 lines in Èwòndó with an explicit moral.
teacher.freedom: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.
teacher.tips: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.

student.intro: Èwòndó tales, proverbs and riddles are literary works in their own right. You will analyse them and you will create your own!
activities: Read the tale provided and identify the 5 stages of its narrative structure.
Identify 3 moral values taught by this tale.
Translate a proverb in Èwòndó into French and explain its figurative meaning.
Write a short tale (15 lines) in Èwòndó with a moral about work or respect.
Memorise: tale = fictional narrative with an educational purpose; proverb = brief formula of collective wisdom.
student.memo: The **oral literature** of **Èwòndó** (tales, proverbs, riddles) transmits the values of the community. The tale has a 5-stage structure. Writing it in Èwòndó draws on all the language skills acquired.

lessons.title: Who are the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)? Identity, language and territory
lessons.anelcac: Cultural areas, cultural identity, settlement
objectives: Name the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where did they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Ewondo community (Mvog Tsung, Mbala): who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group but integrated into a very mixed environment (Basaa, Grassfields, peoples of the North). • Ewondo is spoken in the Centre, the South and the East. • Marriage within the group is forbidden: alliances are made with other groups. • Ancestral land, with no religious value: it was Charles Atangana Ntsama who brought the missionaries there. • Like the Beti as a whole, the group crossed the Sanaga on the mythical serpent and first settled at Ngwa Ekələ, on the Atəməŋgə plateau; ties with these places remain.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the heart of Yaoundé, Efoulan describes itself as a “mixture of peoples”: the Ewondo live there with Basaa, people from the Grassfields and from the North. Like all the Beti, they say they crossed the Sanaga on the back of a mythical snake. Catholic and highly urbanised, they keep the olugu, respect for elders, and the music of the balafon and the tam-tam.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community: its name, its language, its neighbours and its history.

activities.title: I understand the name
activities.instruction: Explain the name the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) give themselves (Efulán məyoŋ) and its meaning.

activities.title: I locate
activities.instruction: On a map, place the community, its region and its neighbours.

activities.title: I trace the history
activities.instruction: On a timeline or a map, draw the migration route told in tradition.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare the origin of this people with that of your own community: 2 similarities, 2 differences.

student.memo: In the heart of Yaoundé, Efoulan describes itself as a “mixture of peoples”: the Ewondo live there with Basaa, people from the Grassfields and from the North. Like all the Beti, they say they crossed the Sanaga on the back of a mythical snake. Catholic and highly urbanised, they keep the olugu, respect for elders, and the music of the balafon and the tam-tam.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
objectives: Identify traditional authorities
Explain how decisions are made
Identifying the rules of deference
lessons.competence: Describe how the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision has to be made for the whole Ewondo village (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “An important decision has to be made for the whole village of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Who decides, and how?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Monarchy, age and kinship organise society; the family deliberates and then approaches the chief, who convenes and decides by consensus. • Among the Beti, an unmarried man does not speak in public and was not entitled to the essani at his death. • A man's inheritance stays in his family. • The olugu, respect for elders, family and blood ties, governs communal life.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Kingship, age and kinship organise society; the family deliberates and then approaches the chief, who convenes the assembly and decides by consensus. Among the Beti, an unmarried man does not speak in public and was not entitled to the essani at his death. A man's inheritance stays within his family.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: How do the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) live together? Who decides, and how do people show respect to one another?

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Describe the path of a decision, from discussion to public announcement.

activities.title: I pick out
activities.instruction: Note down two rules of respect or deference and explain their meaning.

activities.title: I debate
activities.instruction: In groups: what are the advantages of making decisions by consensus?

student.memo: Kingship, age and kinship organise society; the family deliberates and then approaches the chief, who convenes the assembly and decides by consensus. Among the Beti, an unmarried man does not speak in public and was not entitled to the essani at his death. A man's inheritance stays within his family.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Ways of life: culinary practices
objectives: Naming traditional foods and drinks
Describe a preparation
Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), describe how they are prepared and draw out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala).” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kpəm (cassava leaves). • Drinks: palm wine (məjɔg malen). • Men and women: trade (mákit), rearing pigs and poultry.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) eat mainly kpəm. Traditional drinks: məjɔg malen. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out what the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) traditionally eat and drink.

activities.title: I match
activities.instruction: Link each dish to the group's activities (agriculture, fishing, livestock rearing…).

activities.title: I present
activities.instruction: Prepare a poster for the class food fair.

student.memo: The Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) eat mainly kpəm. Traditional drinks: məjɔg malen. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Clothing, adornments and crafts of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Ways of life: clothing practices, crafts
objectives: Describe traditional clothing
Identify craft objects and their use
Explain the criteria of beauty
lessons.competence: Describe the clothing, adornments and craft objects of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), and explain their use and value.
lessons.situation: A museum asks you to prepare a display on the clothing and crafts of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, craft objects or photos of craft objects, recycled materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the clothing, adornments and craft objects of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), and explain their use and value.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A museum asks you to prepare a display case on the clothing and crafts of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala).” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How did people dress in the past, and how do they dress today? — Do clothes indicate status or occasion? — What objects are made, from what materials, and for what uses? — What are the criteria of beauty?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Traditional dress is no longer followed: everyone dresses as they wish. • Traditional medicine remains effective and widely used. • Basketry, pottery and sculpture, practised by the ancestors, have disappeared. • Beauty is judged to be relative and personal.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Traditional dress is no longer followed: everyone dresses as they wish. Traditional medicine remains effective and widely used. Basketry, pottery and sculpture, practised by the ancestors, have disappeared.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw and label a garment or craft object of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), stating its material, use and occasion.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Key events: birth, naming, initiation
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
Describe how names are given
Describe the passage to adulthood
lessons.competence: Explain how the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born into a Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) family. How will he or she be named, and how will he or she become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A child has just been born into a Ewondo family (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). How will the child be named, and how will they become an adult?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Everyone names their child as they wish; only the name ŋdəŋhə is reserved for men. • Names are not changed; a pseudonym is sometimes used. • The founding ancestor is called Ataŋgana Esomba. • Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator. • Patrilineal kinship today; the wife joins her husband's family.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Everyone names their child as they wish; only the name ŋdəŋhə is reserved for men. People do not change their name; sometimes a pseudonym is used. The founding ancestor is called Ataŋgana Esomba.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Explain the meaning of three Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) personal names and describe the moment when a child receives their name.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Key events: marriage
objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order
Explain the symbolism of the bride price
Comparing yesterday and today
lessons.competence: Describe the stages of traditional Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) marriage, the bride price items and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) woman. Which steps will he have to follow?
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, props for the staging.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Ewondo woman (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Which steps will he have to follow?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Patrilineal kinship today; the wife joins her husband's family. • No one declares a boy a man or a girl a woman: each person asserts themselves. • Stages: ekud mbɛ́ (“knocking at the door”, because the boy used to enter through the window), then nsi lí alug, the marriage request in which the bride price list is handed over. • Bride price: red wine, a large goat (ekut kabet) for the young woman's parents, aŋgámbá wán.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Steps: ekud mbɛ́ (“knocking at the door”, because the boy used to enter through the window), then nsi lí alug, the marriage request at which the bride price list is handed over. Bride price: red wine, a large goat (ekut kabet) for the girl's parents, aŋgámbá wán.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: In a group, role-play the marriage request among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), then explain the meaning of two items of the bride price.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: leisure, traditional dances
objectives: Identify dances and their occasions
Describe a dance and its instruments
Perform the dance
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares an Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), choose the most representative one, describe it, draw out its cultural significance and act it out.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Participation in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Ewondo dance performance (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) for the cultural day.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Music: miŋkúl (tam-tam) and məjaŋ (balafon). • Dances: asiko ŋnam, osilaa, ɲəʒ. • The old community festivals have disappeared.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), the traditional dances (asiko ŋnam, osilaa, ɲəʒ) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam ŋkúl, balafon məjaŋ.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a dance of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: traditional economy
objectives: Identify economic activities
Explain the division of tasks
Explain access to land
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). First you need to understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A development project wants to help the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). First, we need to understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men and women: trade (mákit), rearing of pigs and poultry. • Land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought by reaching an agreement with the neighbours to draw up the papers. • Basketry, pottery and sculpture, practised by the ancestors, have disappeared.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men and women: trade (mákit), pig and poultry rearing. Land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought by reaching an agreement with the neighbours to draw up the papers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: symbolism, rites, taboos
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
Identify sacred places
Explain the role of taboos
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Which places and rules must they absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A visitor arrives among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). What places and rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The group is Catholic and no longer has ancestor worship. • Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator. • Taboos: incest, contempt for elders. • Transgressions led to quarantine (mimbok mi dzal); incest required an expiatory rite with a goat or a sheep.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The group is Catholic and no longer has ancestor worship. Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) (3 places or rules to respect, with the reason for each).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ewondo
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
Introducing yourself
Counting from 1 to 10
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in sharing the kola nuts while counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “You are visiting a Ewondo family (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the kola nuts by counting.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Ewondo. • Greeting formulas: Masuk = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Mbembə kiri = morning greeting (one person); Mini vuman = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Fɔg, Bɛ, Lɛ, ɲi, tan. • The founding ancestor is called Ataŋgana Esomba. • The chiefdom has been passed on since Charles Atangana Ntsama.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ewondo are the first steps towards communicating with the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
